Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

vignette: When Mara first stepped onto the highway that autumn, the war‑zone memories she carried from the front lines were still fresh, and the long hours on the bus route began to feel like a daily reenactment. She remembered a sudden explosion that had shattered her sense of safety, the sound of distant artillery, and the dizzying rush of adrenaline that had taken over her body. In the weeks after that night, the very act of driving became a trigger for her; the stress of tight schedules, the dizziness that crept in when she had to reverse out of a tight lane, and the unpredictability of the crowds at each stop all set off a rapid chain of reactions. She found herself constantly scanning the bus for any sign of danger, even as the driver’s cabin remained quiet and the passengers were merely waiting for their stops. The physical reactivity—shaking hands, racing heart, the need to keep her back against the side of the bus so she could see the entire interior—was the most visceral reminder of the battle. The thought that her life had been destroyed by that trauma, and that she was no longer capable of the skills that had once defined her, flooded her mind each time she felt the wind shift or a passenger's laugh cut too close. These triggers did not simply precede the threat; they intensified it, and in turn, the threat amplified her negative appraisals. The more she scanned, the deeper her conviction grew that she was doomed to feel unsafe forever. Mara's belief that she had lost her meaning and her sense of capability only made the threat more urgent. After a particularly jarring incident—when a commuter stepped too close to her as she was pulling over to let them exit—she felt a surge of fear so intense it made her heart pound against her ribs. In that moment, the idea that her life had been destroyed seemed almost an unavoidable truth; the threat of danger was now intertwined with her conviction that she could not handle even the simplest tasks. Her negative appraisal that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her began to dictate her next steps. She stopped accepting passenger requests to change her route, even though the bus had enough space. She began to avoid any situation that might provoke dizziness or a feeling of unpredictability, such as driving in heavy traffic or taking shortcuts to cut time. These avoidance behaviors, born from the cycle of negative appraisals, reinforced her sense that her world was shrinking and that she was powerless. The persistent sense of threat that Mara carried on every shift fed back into her negative appraisals. Each time she found herself scanning, she would hear in her head the same refrain: “I am not safe. I am not capable.” The constant threat convinced her that nothing could be trusted, that the bus was a potential trap. The very act of looking for danger at each stop—her eyes darting across the window, her mind racing—reinforced her conviction that life was destroyed and that no meaning could be found in her daily routine. Moreover, the threat itself became a trigger; the sight of a crowded stop or a sudden honk of a horn would send her dizziness spiraling, forcing her to lean back against the wall of the bus to feel anchored. In the safety of the side, she could see the whole room, but she still felt unsafe because the threat remained in her mind. Each cycle of threat, negative appraisal, and trigger only tightened the loop, pulling her deeper into a state of chronic alertness that left her exhausted both physically and emotionally. Mara has been working as a bus driver for three years now, but she no longer enjoys the drive. The once proud feeling she had when she successfully navigated a tricky route has been replaced by a nagging doubt. She often feels that her life is meaningless and that she has no control over the world she once moved with confidence. This has led her to miss work, to avoid routes that take her through unfamiliar neighborhoods, and to refuse to accept new responsibilities that would have required her to trust herself. Her relationships with passengers have become strained; she feels detached, as if she is just going through the motions. The last time she saw a child in the bus, waving a toy car at her from the window, her heart clenched. She could have smiled, but she avoided eye contact, feeling that even a small moment of joy could bring her dizziness or a sudden, unexplained rush of fear. The day Mara finally reached out for help was when she realized that her own driving routine had become a source of pain rather than purpose. She was afraid that if she did not address the spiraling cycle, she might lose her job entirely, and that would be the final blow to the sense of meaning she had already lost. She hopes to regain a sense of safety and to find a way to feel capable again, so that the bus becomes a vehicle of movement rather than a cage that holds her in constant dread.
